title: Hydrolysis of cane sugar
body: A student dissolves cane sugar (sucrose) in water and finds, using a polarimeter, that the solution rotates plane-polarised light to the right. She then boils the solution with a little dilute hydrochloric acid for some time. On measuring again, she finds that the solution now rotates plane-polarised light to the left. Her teacher explains that sucrose has been hydrolysed into an equimolar mixture of two monosaccharides, D-(+)-glucose and D-(-)-fructose, which in sucrose are joined by a glycosidic linkage between C1 of alpha-D-glucose and C2 of beta-D-fructose. The specific rotation of glucose is +52.5 degrees and that of fructose is -92.4 degrees. The product mixture is called invert sugar.
